'''''Rhododendron maximum''''' is a species of ''[[Rhododendron]]'' native to the [[Appalachians]] of eastern [[North America]], from [[Alabama]] north to coastal [[Nova Scotia]]. Its common names include '''great laurel''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=RHMA4|taxon=Rhododendron maximum|access-date=21 October 2015}}</ref> '''great rhododendron''', '''rosebay rhododendron''', '''American rhododendron''' and '''big rhododendron'''.

==Description==
''Rhododendron maximum'' is an [[evergreen]] [[shrub]] growing to {{convert|4|m|ft|abbr=on}}, rarely {{convert|10|m|ft|abbr=on}}, tall. The [[leaf|leaves]] are {{convert|9|–|19|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|2|–|4|cm|in|abbr=on}} broad.<ref name=mbg>{{cite web| title= Rhododendron maximum | publisher=[[Missouri Botanical Garden]] | url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=279985 | access-date=2019-08-27}}</ref> The [[flower]]s are {{convert|2.5-3|cm|in|abbr=on}} diameter, white, pink or pale purple, often with small greenish-yellow spots. The [[fruit]] is a dry [[capsule (fruit)|capsule]] {{convert|15|–|20|mm|in|abbr=on}} long, containing numerous small [[seed]]s. The leaves can be poisonous. Leaves are sclerophyllous, simple, alternate, and oblong (10 to 30 cm long, 5 to 8 cm wide). It retains its waxy, deep-green leaves for up to 8 years, but once shed are slow to decompose. It produces large, showy, white to purple flowers each June and July.<ref name=mbg/>

==Distribution and habitat==
Rosebay rhododendron is the most frequently occurring and dominant species of ''Rhododendron'' in the southern Appalachian region,<ref>{{cite book | last=Swanson | first=R. E. | year=1994 | title=A Field Guide to the Trees and Shrubs of the Southern Appalachians | publisher=The Johns Hopkins University Press | location=Baltimore, MD | page=399}}</ref> and occurs occasionally on [[Mesic habitat|mesic]] hill-slopes throughout the upper Piedmont Crescent of the Southeastern United States.

==Ecology==
[[File:Nature's Thermometers.jpg|thumb|The leaves responding to subfreezing temperatures by curling.]]
Approximately 12,000 square miles in the southern Appalachians are occupied by this species<ref>{{cite book | last=Dobbs | first=M. M. | year=1995 | title=Spatial and temporal distribution of the evergreen understory in the southern Appalachians | type=M. Sci. Thesis | publisher=University of Georgia | location=Athens, GA | page=100 }}</ref> where it dominates the understory. This species has historically been confined to riparian areas and other mesic sites but takes advantage of disturbed areas where it is present to advance onto sub-mesic sites. It prefers deep well-drained acid soils high in organic matter where it produces a thick, peat-like humus. It prefers low to medium light conditions for optimum carbon gain, and has a tremendous capacity for avoiding cavitation during freeze-thaw cycles.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Lipp | first1=C. C. | first2=E. T. | last2=Nilsen | year=1997 | title=The impact of subcanopy light environment on the hydraulic vulnerability of Rhododendron maximum to freeze-thaw cycles and drought | journal=Plant, Cell and Environment | volume=20 | issue=10 | pages=1.264–1.272| doi=10.1046/j.1365-3040.1997.d01-22.x | doi-access=free }}</ref>  Where extensive overstory mortality has eliminated most of the overstory, this species forms a thick and continuous subcanopy known locally as 'laurel slicks' or 'laurel hells'. Rosebay rhododendron is an important structural and functional component of southern Appalachian forest ecosystems. What is not clear is whether or not we are in a period of advancement or retreat for this species. For example, on poorly drained sites on ridge or upper slope positions, large areas of rosebay rhododendron, particularly at the high elevations, have recently died out presumably due to the ''[[Phytophthora]]'' fungus, or due to recent prolonged periods of below-average precipitation. Yet, rosebay rhododendron now occupies sites that historically were free of evergreen understory. There are still important questions to be answered regarding this species to completely understand its role in forest understories.

In North Carolina, US, ''[[Pestalotiopsis]]'' which is a [[genus]] of [[ascomycete]] fungi causes grey-brown spots on the living leaves.<ref name="Maharachchikumbura2014">{{cite journal |last1=Maharachchikumbura |first1=S.S.N. |last2=Hyde |first2=K.D. |last3=Groenewald |first3=J.Z. |last4=Xu |first4=J. |last5=Crous |first5=P.W. |title=''Pestalotiopsis'' revisited |journal=Studies in Mycology |date=September 2014 |volume=79 |pages=121–186|doi=10.1016/j.simyco.2014.09.005 |pmid=25492988 |pmc=4255583 }}</ref>

==Reproduction==
Rosebay rhododendron is [[Clonal colony|clonal]]. It is capable, however, of reproducing both [[Vegetative reproduction|vegetatively]] and sexually. It reproduces vegetatively through a process called '[[layering (horticulture)|layering]]' where it produces roots from above ground woody parts when in contact with the forest floor. The fruit is produced from showy flowers from March to August. The fruit is an oblong capsule that ripens in the fall, and splits along the sides soon after ripening to release large numbers of minute seed (c. 400 per capsule).<ref>{{cite book | last=Schopmeyer | first=C. S. | year=1974 | title=Seeds of woody plants in the United States | publisher=USDA Forest Service | series=Agricultural Handbook No. 45Q | page=883 }}</ref>  Microsite requirements for seed germination are relatively specific (e.g., high in organic matter such as rotting logs); hence, the majority of reproduction is vegetative resulting in a clonal distribution.

==Cultivation==
[[File:Rhododendron maximum regrowth.JPG|thumb|Cultivated plant]]
Seeds from rosebay rhododendron are minute and it is estimated that approximately 11 million are contained in 1 kg. Commercial seed production is generally from cultivated hybrids. Seeds from wild sources are not commonly sold commercially. Rosebay rhododendron is a slow-growing shrub and has a very high sprout potential. If mechanical removal is attempted in the case of forest management, extremely high densities are attained by this species in a matter of a few years. Prescribed fire has also been used to control this species but with limited success.<ref>{{cite book | last1=Clinton | first1=B. D. | first2=J. M. | last2=Vose | year=2000 | chapter=Plant succession and community restoration following felling and burning in the southern Appalachian Mountains | pages=22–29 | editor=W. K. Moser & C. F. Moser | title=Fire and forest ecology: innovative silviculture and vegetation management | series=Tall Timbers Fire Ecology Conference Proceedings | volume=21 | publisher=Tall Timbers Research Station | location=Tallahassee, FL}}</ref>

==Uses==
Rosebay rhododendron is a striking and aesthetically pleasing feature of mesic southern Appalachian forests. It is one of the largest and hardiest rhododendrons grown commercially. Several cultivars with white to purple flowers have been selected for the horticultural trade.<ref>{{cite book | last1=Brown | first1=C. L. | first2=L. K. | last2=Kirkman | year=1990 | title=Trees of Georgia and Adjacent States | publisher=Timber Press | location=Portland, OR | page=292}}</ref> Where it occurs naturally, it produces a showy, white, pink, or light purple flower primarily in June, but occurs from March into August. Rosebay rhododendron maintains deep-green foliage year round. This species affords protection to steep watersheds and shelter for wildlife. The wood is very hard and is occasionally used for specialty wood products.

==Detrimental effects==
For all its prized qualities as a naturally occurring component of the landscape or as plantings in residential and commercial landscaping, rosebay rhododendron can have an inhibitory effect on regeneration of other plant species. There is some evidence to suggest that due to fire suppression and the absence of other cultural activities (i.e., mountain-land grazing), this species has advanced beyond the [[Mesic habitat|mesic]] forest sites into sub-mesic understories.<ref>{{cite book | last=Dobbs | first=M. M. | year=1998 | title=Dynamics of the evergreen understory at Coweeta | publication-place=Hydrologic Laboratory, North Carolina | type=PhD Dissertation | publisher=University of Georgia | location=Athens GA | page=179}}</ref> The significance of this movement onto previously unoccupied sites centers around the impacts of rosebay rhododendron on plant succession<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Clinton | first1=B. D. | first2=J. M. | last2=Vose | year=1996 | title=Effects of Rhododendron maximum L. on Acer rubrum L. seedling establishment | journal=Castanea | volume=61 | issue=1 | pages=38–45}}</ref> and resource availability.<ref name=nils01>{{cite journal | last1=Nilsen | first1=E. T. | first2=B. D. | last2=Clinton | first3=T. T. | last3=Lei | first4=K. | last4=Miller | first5=S. W. | last5=Semones | first6=J. F. | last6=Walker | year=2001 | title=Does Rhododendron maximum L. (Ericaceae) reduce the availability of resources above and belowground for canopy tree seedlings? | journal=American Midland Naturalist | volume=145 | issue=2 | pages=325–343| doi=10.1674/0003-0031(2001)145[0325:DRMLER]2.0.CO;2 | s2cid=7021773 }}</ref>  Rosebay rhododendron is associated with reduced woody and herbaceous seedling abundance throughout its range, and hence poses a serious impediment to the production of wood products. The mechanism(s) by which rosebay rhododendron reduces seedling survival has been the subject of much debate. Possible sources of inhibition include [[allelopathy]], competition for resources including light, physical and chemical attributes of the forest floor and soil, and interactions between some or all sources.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Nilsen | first1=E. T. | first2=J. F. | last2=Walker | first3=O. K. | last3=Miller | first4=S. W. | last4=Semones | first5=T. T. | last5=Lei | first6=B. D. | last6=Clinton | year=1999 | title=Inhibition of seedling survival under Rhododendron maximum (Ericaceae): could allelopathy be a cause? | journal=American Journal of Botany | volume=86 | issue=11 | pages=1.597–1.605| doi=10.2307/2656796 | jstor=2656796 }}</ref><ref name=nils01/>
